h1:
Prasat Khao Noi Si Chomphu
An Ancient Khmer Temple on a Hill
intro: If you like quiet, uncrowded historical sites, Prasat Khao Noi Si Chomphu in Aranyaprathet is worth a stop. It's a Khmer temple over a thousand years old sitting on top of Khao Noi hill, so you'll have to climb some stairs — but once you're up there, the old brick tower and the wide view over the border country make the tired legs worth it. This article walks you through what's up there, how to make the climb, what time it opens, and where else to head nearby.

blocks.html: Prasat Khao Noi Si Chomphu is one of the oldest Khmer temples in Thailand. It sits on top of Khao Noi hill in Khlong Nam Sai sub-district, Aranyaprathet, only about 1 kilometer from the Thai–Cambodian border. Locals in Sa Kaeo just call it 'Prasat Khao Noi.' The 'Si Chomphu' part comes from the name of the hill and the temple beside it — it doesn't mean the temple itself is pink, which is a mix-up a lot of people make.

blocks.text: What is Prasat Khao Noi Si Chomphu, and how old is it?

blocks.html: The temple is thought to have been built around the 7th century AD, during the Chenla–Dvaravati period — even before the age of Angkor Wat. It was later restored in the 10th century. It started out as a Hindu religious site, and all in all it's about 1,300–1,400 years old, which makes it one of the oldest traces of Khmer civilization found anywhere in Thailand.

What makes historians pay attention is the stone inscription found here. It records the Mahasakarat year 559, corresponding to 637 AD, which is considered the oldest dated inscription ever discovered in Thailand. The Fine Arts Department registered the site as a historical monument back in 1935, then came back to excavate and restore it again around 1989.

Originally the temple had three brick towers — the north tower, the central tower, and the south sanctuary — all built from brick laid without mortar. After more than a thousand years, the central tower is the one whose shape is still clearly recognizable, while the other two are reduced to bases and earthen mounds, so you'll need a bit of imagination as you walk around. Even so, the old brick and the masonry have their own kind of charm.

blocks.text: Climbing the 254 steps — get your legs ready

blocks.html: The temple sits on top of Khao Noi, which rises about 100–130 meters above the flat ground. The main route up is a flight of around 254 steps, climbing gradually with landings here and there to catch your breath. If you don't exercise much, you'll find it tiring enough — take it slow, bring water, and go in the morning or late afternoon, which is far more comfortable than the harsh midday sun.

If the stairs really aren't for you, there's an alternative: you can drive around the hill past Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu and go up about another kilometer, then walk roughly 250 meters more to reach the temple. That cuts out most of the stairs and works well if you're bringing older relatives along — though the last stretch still involves a bit of an uphill walk.

items: Shoes — wear sneakers or shoes you can walk comfortably in; some sections of the steps are uneven.
Water — there's no shop up top, so bring your own.
Timing — early before it gets hot, or late afternoon when the sun is softer, is easiest to walk and best for photos.
Rainy season — the steps and stone surface can get slippery, so watch your footing.

blocks.title: A small tip
blocks.html: Once you reach the top, don't rush back down. Walk around the tower and find an angle looking out over the fields and the line of hills on the Cambodian side. In the late afternoon, when the light goes soft, is when the view is at its best for the day.

Once you reach the summit, the first thing you'll see is the central brick tower standing prominently in the middle of the old temple grounds, with the bases of the other two towers around it to explore. It's fairly quiet up there, with big trees for shade and far fewer visitors than the more famous temples elsewhere, so you get a kind of calm that's hard to find.

The other bonus is the view. Because the temple sits on a hilltop, you can see rice fields, villages, and the line of hills along the border stretching out wide. It's a spot a lot of people like to sit and rest in the breeze before heading back down. On the same grounds there's also Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu, where you can stop to make merit afterward.

items.name: The central tower
items.blurb: The brick tower in the best condition, showing the old masonry and the form of an early Khmer temple. This is the main photo spot.

items.name: North & south tower bases
items.blurb: The bases of the other two towers, now just brick mounds. Walking around helps you picture the original layout that once had three towers.

items.name: Summit viewpoint
items.blurb: Looking out over the fields and the border hills, with a cool breeze — a good place to rest in the late afternoon.

items.name: Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu
items.blurb: A temple on the same grounds. Stop to pay respects and rest before climbing up to or down from the ruins.

blocks.text: How to get there, opening hours, and entry fee

blocks.html: The temple is about 12 kilometers south of Aranyaprathet town. Most people drive their own car or motorbike, since public transport is hard to reach it by. Coming from Sa Kaeo city it's about an hour-plus drive. There are signs along the way for the entrance to Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu — turn in and park at the temple lot at the bottom, then start the climb from there.

items: Opening hours — open for visits during daylight, ideally around 8:00 AM–5:00 PM, since it's an outdoor historical site; avoid going up near dark.
Parking — park at the Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu lot below and walk up.
Time needed — roughly 1–1.5 hours including the climb up, the visit, and coming down.

blocks.title: What to know about the border
blocks.html: The temple is very close to the Thai–Cambodian border. The temple itself can be visited as usual, but the border situation in this area can change from time to time. Before you actually go, check the latest news and ask locals or the TAT office in Sa Kaeo for peace of mind, and don't wander outside the areas open to visitors.

blocks.text: More to do nearby in a single day

blocks.html: Prasat Khao Noi Si Chomphu doesn't take long to visit, so it fits well into a one-day trip around Aranyaprathet. Here are the nearby spots that people like to pair it with.

items.name: Rong Kluea Market
items.blurb: A large border market about 10 kilometers from the temple. Browse for cheap second-hand clothes, food, and everyday goods.

items.name: Khlong Luek–Poipet Border
items.blurb: The permanent Aranyaprathet–Poipet border crossing, in the same area as Rong Kluea Market.

items.name: Prasat Sdok Kok Thom
items.blurb: The most complete sandstone Khmer temple in eastern Thailand, in Khok Sung district. A must for history fans.

blocks.html: If you're planning a full day, start at Prasat Khao Noi Si Chomphu in the morning while it's still cool, then move on to Prasat Sdok Kok Thom or Rong Kluea Market in the late morning to afternoon, and finish with some good food in Aranyaprathet town.

blocks.text: Who it's for, and who it isn't

items: Good fit — people who love history and Khmer temples, like quiet, uncrowded places, and don't mind climbing stairs.
Good fit — photographers who want an angle of ancient ruins paired with hill views.
Think it over — if you can't manage the stairs, or you're bringing small children or elderly people, take the road around the hill instead.
Think it over — if you're expecting a big, intact temple like Angkor Wat, not much remains here; you have to enjoy the atmosphere more than the grandeur.

faq.q: Is Prasat Khao Noi Si Chomphu actually pink?
faq.a: No. The temple is an old brick tower the color of its material. The 'Si Chomphu' (pink) part of the name comes from the name of the hill and Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu beside it — it has nothing to do with the color of the temple itself.

faq.q: How many steps are there, and is it tiring?
faq.a: The main route up is about 254 steps with landings here and there. Most people can manage the climb, but it's fairly tiring. If the stairs aren't for you, there's a road around the hill past the temple that goes up about 1 kilometer, after which you walk roughly 250 meters more.

faq.q: What time does it open, and is there an entry fee?
faq.a: It's an outdoor historical site, free to enter with no ticket. It's best to visit during daylight, around 8:00 AM–5:00 PM, and avoid going near dark since the path has no lighting.

faq.q: How do you get there, and is it far from town?
faq.a: It's in Khlong Nam Sai sub-district, Aranyaprathet, about 12 kilometers from the town center. Most people drive their own car or motorbike, since public transport is hard to reach it by. Park at the Wat Khao Noi Si Chomphu lot and walk up.

faq.q: The temple is right by the border — is it safe to visit?
faq.a: The temple sits about 1 kilometer from the Thai–Cambodian border and can normally be visited, but the border situation can change from time to time. Before you go, check the latest news and ask locals or the TAT office in Sa Kaeo, and don't wander outside the areas open to visitors.
